title: SafeLab: Safe Robot Learning Through Simulation and Recovery
one_liner: A benchmark that teaches robots not just to succeed at lab tasks, but to stay safe while doing them by catching and fixing execution drift before it causes damage.
lead: Robots working in science labs face a harsh reality: a tiny mistake during a delicate task like pouring liquid or handling glassware can cause permanent damage. Most robot training ignores this — they measure success only by reaching the goal, not by staying safe along the way. SafeLab flips this: it creates realistic lab tasks where the robot must remain safe throughout the entire motion, and trains recovery moves that catch the robot when it starts to drift.

problem.h2: Lab robots succeed but break things
paras: Most robot tasks in the real world ask for two different things, but only measure one. You need the robot arm to reach its target (move the beaker from here to there) AND stay safe the whole time (never tilt the beaker past 15 degrees, never press harder than the glassware can handle). Standard benchmarks only grade task success: did you reach the goal?

A beginner's approach: train the robot to copy successful human demonstrations. If a human moved the beaker without spilling, the robot watches and learns to do the same. But during actual execution, the robot drifts. Its gripper closes slightly too tight. The arm moves an inch too far. These small errors pile up, and by the time the task is done, the beaker has tipped and shattered. The policy succeeded at the goal, but failed catastrophically at safety.

callout.html: Lab robots are trained to reach goals, not to stay safe while reaching them. When small execution errors happen, no one teaches the robot how to catch and fix itself.

steps.text: Build a computer model of real lab equipment, liquids, and physics that accurately predicts when things spill or break.
Automatically create safe demonstrations by having software teleoperate the simulated robot, collecting 6,400 successful, safe trajectories.
Let the robot learn from those demonstrations to copy the basic motion — reaching the goal while staying mostly safe.
Compare task success (did it reach the goal?) to safe success (did it stay safe the whole time?). Spot tasks where the robot succeeds unsafely.
Add a second learning layer that, during execution, detects when drift is happening and applies small nudges to keep the robot on the safe path.

paras: The paper's core move is adding a second policy layer that runs during execution and catches drift. The base policy commits to a path learned from demonstrations. But when the robot actually moves, small errors accumulate: the arm is a millimeter off, the gripper pressure varies, the tilt creeps. The recovery layer watches these small errors and applies tiny, bounded corrections—nudge the arm 0.5 centimeters back, reduce gripper pressure by 2 percent—to steer the robot back to a safe trajectory.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Safe Success Rate
hidden.name: Safe Success Rate
paras: The paper measures a new kind of success: did the robot reach the goal AND stay safe the entire trajectory? This is the Safe Success Rate. A trajectory could reach the goal (task success) but violate a safety constraint like tilting the beaker past the safe angle or pressing with too much force (unsafe). SafeLab finds the gap: many imitation-trained policies succeed at the goal 90 percent of the time, but only succeed safely 50 percent of the time.

To estimate safety, SafeLab simulates the task and checks every frame: is the arm pressing too hard? Is the beaker tilted past the limit? Did liquid start to spill? By the end of the trajectory, either the robot stayed safe (Safe Success Rate is 100 percent) or it breached a safety constraint somewhere (Safe Success Rate is 0 percent).

heat.caption: Darker means more trajectory breaches. Top: naive policy (high task success, low safe success). Bottom: with residual RL (safe success rises).

reads.html: Task Success Rate is the percent of times the robot reached the goal. Safe Success Rate is the percent of times it reached the goal without violating any safety constraint (tilt, force, spillage) at any point in the trajectory.

SafeLab evaluates a bounded residual RL agent that learns corrections to a base imitation policy, measuring the gap between task success and Safe Success Rate across 64 tasks, revealing systematic unsafe-but-successful trajectories in liquid handling, force-limited actuation, and bimanual manipulation.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: catching drift in time
paras: The mechanism hinges on timing and correction magnitude. When a robot executes a learned policy, it makes small errors at each step — the gripper doesn't close to exactly the right force, the arm overshoots by 5 millimeters. In isolation these are tiny, but over 100 steps they compound into a large drift that crosses a safety boundary. The recovery layer samples the actual robot state at each step and compares it to the ideal trajectory the base policy expected. If the arm is 8 millimeters off when it should be 2 millimeters off, the recovery layer applies a bounded correction: move back 4 millimeters, not the full 8. This keeps corrections small enough that the robot still makes progress toward the goal, but large enough to prevent drift from spiraling.

Why small corrections work: the base policy already learned a mostly safe path from demonstrations. It is not asking the robot to learn a whole new strategy, only to apply tiny corrective nudges when it starts to drift. These nudges are bounded—never more than a small fraction of the maximum actuator movement—so they cannot overshoot and cause a different safety breach. Over the entire trajectory, many small corrections accumulate to keep the robot on the safe path, even though individual steps are slightly off the ideal motion.

stages.s: recovery layer bounds and applies correction

math.words: final action equals the learned policy output plus a bounded correction term that is proportional to the current state error but never exceeds a safety limit
symbols: the actual action sent to the robot
the action the learned policy recommends
the error between actual state and expected state
clamp the value to stay between negative and positive limits

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Base policy says: move arm forward 10 millimeters. Expected state if perfect: arm is 2mm off from ideal. Actual state: arm is 8mm off.
Error e = 8mm - 2mm = 6mm. Correction gain k = 0.5, maximum correction c_max = 3mm.
Raw correction: k * e = 0.5 * 6mm = 3mm. After clipping to c_max=3mm: clip(3, -3, 3) = 3mm.
Final action: a_final = 10mm + 3mm = 13mm. Robot corrects toward the ideal, but the 13mm is large enough to pull back, small enough to not overshoot.

math.note: The clip function is the key: it prevents corrections from becoming so large they introduce new safety problems while still being large enough to catch drift.

charts.title: Imitation policy only
charts.note: Robot reaches the goal most of the time, but safety is poor; liquid-handling tasks are especially unsafe.

charts.title: With residual RL corrections
charts.note: Safe success rises 29 percentage points (from 52% to 81%); task success barely drops; liquid handling becomes safe.

items.html: If k is large, the recovery layer overreacts to small errors, jerking the robot and violating constraints itself. A correction meant to fix a 1-millimeter drift accidentally induces a 20-millimeter one.
If c_max is tiny (say, 0.2 millimeters), the robot cannot catch large drift. By the time an error is 10 millimeters, the corrections are too small to matter, and drift spirals anyway.

If the simulation does not accurately model how glassware breaks or when liquid spills, then SafeLab misidentifies which trajectories are safe. The recovered policy then trains to be safe in simulation but unsafe in reality.

Tune k and c_max together through safety-aware training: learn the correction layer specifically to maximize safe success while minimizing task loss. The paper uses bounded residual RL, which does exactly this—it optimizes both coefficients to find the right balance.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple simulated pouring task: a robot arm must move a beaker from one position to another without tilting it past 30 degrees or pressing harder than 2 newtons. Start with a learned policy trained on human demonstrations. First, run it 20 times and measure: how many times does it reach the goal? Of those successes, how many stayed within the tilt and force limits the entire trajectory? You should see the gap (task success much higher than safe success). Then train a small residual RL layer on top, learning when to apply small arm corrections. Run the policy 20 times again and measure safe success. The gap should shrink by at least 15 percentage points.
demo.closing: The irreversibility of lab mistakes is the core: a shattered beaker cannot be un-shattered, and the best safety measure is catching the mistake before it happens, not recovering after.
